While I can't side with Keynes' attempted solutions for economic woes back in the thirties, I can't fault his basic analysis. With automation being so effective, it takes a tiny fraction of the population to grow and manufacture the things we need, which leaves most of economic circulation dependent on the things we want. And when people are at all conservative on those, it means there's simply no demand for those jobs they might fill. His solution was a patch, and since then things have become more efficient and more patches have been applied to the point that there's more patchwork than actual economy.

If we could both deconstruct this horrible government and bring back the old-fashioned ideas of charity and responsibility, there would be sufficiently low prices on food and other staples and enough charity to cover everyone. I'm not sure we'd be able to march back to that point at this time.

I think the construction of a basic income system is inevitable at this point (and will stay that way until we achieve Abundance - but that's another rant). I'm kind of okay with it; applied well, it would require far less overhead than the mess of systems we have now. The problem is it's unlikely to be applied well and is more potentially exploitable than our current systems, which are already rife with corruption. There are also lots of questions as to what should be considered "basic". Basic clothes and food? Eh, okay. Basic housing? We've seen what public housing rapidly turns into. Basic cash income? Yeah, like that won't be abused. Basic healthcare? Also something we've seen turn to shit. Politicians promising to increase the Dole in exchange for votes? Bread and circuses, and Rome will fall again.

It'd be really nice to figure out a way to implement a no-nonsense system with a minimum of potential corruption. Good luck though.
